_about: Names, descriptions, layers and colors used by the anatomy viewer. Edit freely; the app reloads this file when it regains focus. Geometry lives in the geometry-*.bin files and is matched by id. A part can override its color with "color" and its text with "description".

regions.name: Head
regions.description: The 22 bones of the skull with the mandible, teeth and hyoid, the brain, the eyes and ears, and the muscles of the face, jaw and scalp.

regions.name: Neck
regions.description: The muscles of the neck and throat, the larynx and thyroid cartilage, and the great vessels between the head and the chest.

regions.name: Vertebral column
regions.description: Seven cervical, twelve thoracic and five lumbar vertebrae above the sacrum, separated by intervertebral discs. Its S-shaped curves absorb load and keep the head balanced over the pelvis.

regions.name: Chest
regions.description: The ribs, costal cartilages and sternum, the heart and lungs, the great vessels, and the muscles of the chest wall and upper back.

regions.name: Shoulder girdle
regions.description: The clavicles and scapulae connect the arms to the trunk. Only the clavicle joins the axial skeleton, which gives the shoulder its wide range of motion.

regions.name: Abdomen
regions.description: The stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas, spleen and kidneys, the abdominal vessels, and the muscles of the abdominal wall and lower back.

regions.name: Right upper limb

regions.name: Pelvis
regions.description: The two hip bones, the bladder and reproductive organs, and the muscles of the hip, buttock and pelvic floor. With the sacrum the hip bones form the bony pelvis.

frontal.description: Forms the forehead, the roofs of the orbits and the front of the cranial floor. The frontal sinuses sit behind the brow ridges.

parietal.description: Paired bones forming the sides and roof of the cranium. They meet each other at the sagittal suture and the frontal bone at the coronal suture.

occipital.description: Forms the back and base of the cranium. The spinal cord passes through the foramen magnum, and the occipital condyles rest on the atlas.

temporal.description: Houses the organs of hearing and balance in its petrous part. Carries the ear canal, the mastoid process and the socket of the jaw joint.

sphenoid.description: The butterfly-shaped keystone of the cranial base, in contact with every other cranial bone. The sella turcica on its upper surface cradles the pituitary gland.

ethmoid.description: A light, spongy bone between the orbits that forms parts of the nasal cavity and septum. The olfactory nerves pass through its cribriform plate.

nasal.description: Small paired bones forming the bridge of the nose.

lacrimal.description: The tear apparatus: the lacrimal gland above the outer corner of the eye makes tears, which drain from the inner corner through the canaliculi and lacrimal sac into the nasolacrimal duct and the nose.

zygomatic.description: The cheekbone. Forms the prominence of the cheek and parts of the side wall and floor of the orbit.

maxilla.description: The paired upper jaw bones. They carry the upper teeth, form most of the hard palate and the floor of each orbit, and contain the maxillary sinuses.

palatine.description: L-shaped bones forming the back of the hard palate and part of the side wall of the nasal cavity.

concha.description: A scroll-shaped bone on the side wall of the nasal cavity. Its mucous lining warms and moistens inhaled air.

vomer.description: A thin, plowshare-shaped bone forming the lower back part of the nasal septum.

mandible.description: The lower jaw and the only freely movable bone of the skull. It carries the lower teeth and meets the temporal bones at the jaw joints.

hyoid.description: A U-shaped bone that articulates with no other bone. It anchors the tongue and the muscles used for swallowing and speech.

incisor.description: Chisel-shaped front teeth for cutting food.

canine.description: The teeth with the longest roots, for gripping and tearing.

premolar.description: Teeth with two cusps, for crushing and grinding.

molar.description: Broad teeth with several cusps, for grinding. This model has first and second molars; the third molars (wisdom teeth) are not included.

atlas.description: The first cervical vertebra (C1), a ring of bone without a body that carries the skull. Nodding happens at its joints with the occipital bone.

axis.description: The second cervical vertebra (C2). Its tooth-like dens projects up into the ring of the atlas and forms the pivot for turning the head.

cervical.description: Cervical vertebrae have small bodies, forked spinous processes and a hole in each transverse process for the vertebral artery.

thoracic.description: Thoracic vertebrae carry joint facets for the heads of the ribs, have heart-shaped bodies and long spinous processes that slope downward.

lumbar.description: The largest vertebrae, with massive kidney-shaped bodies that carry the weight of the upper body.

sacrum.description: Five fused vertebrae forming a wedge between the hip bones. It passes the weight of the body to the pelvis through the sacroiliac joints. The coccyx below it is not part of this model.

disc.description: A fibrocartilage pad between two vertebral bodies: a tough outer ring (annulus fibrosus) around a gel-like core (nucleus pulposus). The discs absorb load and let the spine bend.

manubrium.description: The top of the sternum. It joins the clavicles and the first ribs; the jugular notch is the dip along its upper edge.

sternum-body.description: The long middle part of the sternum, where the costal cartilages of ribs 2 to 7 attach. It meets the manubrium at the sternal angle.

xiphoid.description: The small lowest part of the sternum, cartilage in youth that gradually turns to bone in adulthood.

rib-true.description: True ribs (1 to 7) reach the sternum through their own costal cartilage.

rib-false.description: False ribs (8 to 10) reach the sternum indirectly, through the cartilage of the rib above.

rib-floating.description: Floating ribs (11 and 12) end freely in the muscles of the flank without reaching the sternum.

costal-cartilage.description: Hyaline cartilage that joins a rib to the sternum and gives the chest wall the flexibility it needs for breathing.

costal-margin.description: The cartilages of ribs 8 to 10 join each other and the seventh cartilage, forming the lower edge of the rib cage (the costal margin).

clavicle.description: The collarbone, an S-shaped strut between the sternum and the scapula. It is the only bony connection between the arm and the trunk.

scapula.description: The shoulder blade, a flat triangular bone on the back of the chest. Its shallow glenoid cavity is the socket of the shoulder joint.

humerus.description: The bone of the upper arm. Its head fits the glenoid cavity of the scapula; its lower end forms the elbow with the radius and ulna.

radius.description: The forearm bone on the thumb side. It rolls around the ulna to turn the palm up and down (supination and pronation).

ulna.description: The forearm bone on the little-finger side. Its olecranon is the point of the elbow.

scaphoid.description: A boat-shaped bone in the proximal row of the wrist on the thumb side. It is the most commonly fractured carpal bone.

lunate.description: A crescent-shaped bone in the middle of the proximal carpal row.

triquetral.description: A pyramid-shaped bone in the proximal carpal row on the little-finger side.

pisiform.description: A pea-shaped sesamoid bone on the palm side of the triquetral, embedded in the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris.

trapezium.description: Distal-row carpal bone at the base of the thumb. Its saddle joint with the first metacarpal lets the thumb reach across the palm.

trapezoid.description: The smallest bone of the distal carpal row, wedged between the trapezium and the capitate.

capitate.description: The largest carpal bone, at the center of the wrist.

hamate.description: A wedge-shaped distal-row bone on the little-finger side, recognized by its hook.

metacarpal.description: The five metacarpals form the palm, numbered I (thumb) to V (little finger). Their heads are the knuckles.

phalanx-hand.description: Finger bones. Each finger has a proximal, a middle and a distal phalanx; the thumb has no middle phalanx.

hip.description: Three bones, the ilium, ischium and pubis, that fuse at the acetabulum, the socket of the hip joint.

femur.description: The thigh bone, the longest and strongest bone in the body. Its head sits in the acetabulum; its lower end forms the knee with the tibia and patella.

patella.description: The kneecap, the largest sesamoid bone in the body. It sits in the tendon of the quadriceps and improves the muscle's leverage.

tibia.description: The shinbone, the main weight-bearing bone of the leg. Its lower end forms the inner ankle bone (medial malleolus).

fibula.description: The slender outer bone of the leg. It carries little weight but anchors muscles and forms the outer ankle bone (lateral malleolus).

talus.description: Passes the weight of the body from the tibia to the foot. No muscles attach to it.

calcaneus.description: The heel bone, the largest tarsal bone. The Achilles tendon attaches to its back.

navicular.description: A boat-shaped tarsal bone on the inner side of the foot, between the talus and the cuneiforms.

cuboid.description: A cube-shaped tarsal bone on the outer side of the foot, in front of the calcaneus.

cuneiform.description: One of three wedge-shaped tarsal bones that build the transverse arch of the foot.

metatarsal.description: The five metatarsals form the middle of the foot, numbered I (big toe) to V (little toe).

phalanx-foot.description: Toe bones. The big toe (hallux) has two phalanges; the other toes have three.

sesamoid-foot.description: Two small bones in the tendons under the head of the first metatarsal. They protect the tendons and take load when the foot pushes off.

skin.description: The skin covers the whole body. Its outer epidermis renews itself every few weeks; the dermis below holds blood vessels, nerve endings, hair follicles and sweat glands.

hair.description: Hair grows from follicles in the dermis. It protects the scalp from sunlight and heat loss and helps sense touch.

muscle.description: A skeletal muscle. Skeletal muscles pull on bones through tendons to move the joints they cross, and are controlled voluntarily.

connective.description: Dense connective tissue: tendons join muscle to bone, ligaments join bone to bone, and aponeuroses and fasciae spread the pull of muscles over a wide area.

heart.description: A four-chambered muscular pump about the size of a fist. The right side sends blood to the lungs; the left side sends it to the rest of the body.

valve.description: A heart valve. Its thin cusps open to let blood through and snap shut to stop it flowing backward.

papillary.description: A finger-like muscle on the inner wall of a ventricle. Through tendinous cords it holds the cusps of the valve closed while the heart contracts.

lung.description: A lobe of the lungs, where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it. The right lung has three lobes, the left lung two, leaving room for the heart.

bronchus.description: The bronchi branch from the trachea into each lung, dividing again and again down to the tiny airways that end in air sacs.

trachea.description: The windpipe, held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage. It runs from the larynx to where it splits into the two main bronchi.

esophagus.description: A muscular tube about 25 cm long that pushes swallowed food from the throat to the stomach in waves.

stomach.description: A muscular sac that stores food and churns it with acid and enzymes before passing it on to the duodenum.

duodenum.description: The first part of the small intestine, a C-shaped loop around the head of the pancreas. Bile and pancreatic juice enter it here.

small-intestine.description: The jejunum and ileum, about six meters of coiled tube in which most nutrients are absorbed.

colon.description: The large intestine absorbs water and salts from what remains of digested food and forms feces.

taenia.description: Three bands of longitudinal muscle along the colon. They are shorter than the colon itself, which gathers it into pouches.

appendix.description: A narrow, finger-like pouch from the start of the large intestine, rich in lymphoid tissue.

rectum.description: The last part of the large intestine, which stores feces before they leave the body.

liver.description: The largest internal organ. It processes nutrients from the gut, makes bile and many blood proteins, stores energy and breaks down toxins.

gallbladder.description: A small pear-shaped sac under the liver that stores and concentrates bile.

pancreas.description: A gland behind the stomach. It releases digestive enzymes into the duodenum and the hormones insulin and glucagon into the blood.

spleen.description: Filters the blood, removes worn-out red blood cells and stores immune cells.

kidney.description: Each kidney filters about 180 liters of blood plasma a day, keeping what the body needs and passing the rest to the bladder as urine.

adrenal.description: A gland on top of each kidney that makes adrenaline, cortisol and aldosterone.

ureter.description: A muscular tube that carries urine from a kidney to the bladder.

bladder.description: A stretchy muscular sac that stores urine.

urethra.description: The tube that carries urine from the bladder out of the body; in men it also carries semen.

prostate.description: A gland below the bladder that surrounds the urethra and adds fluid to semen.

seminal.description: A gland behind the bladder that produces most of the fluid in semen.

testis.description: Produces sperm and the hormone testosterone.

epididymis.description: A coiled tube behind each testis where sperm mature and are stored.

penis.description: Made of three columns of erectile tissue: two corpora cavernosa and the corpus spongiosum around the urethra, which ends in the glans.

thymus.description: A gland behind the sternum where T cells of the immune system mature. It is largest in childhood.

eye.description: The eyeball focuses light onto the retina, which turns it into nerve signals carried by the optic nerve.

ear.description: The visible outer ear, a frame of elastic cartilage covered by skin, which funnels sound into the ear canal.

gingiva.description: The gums, a firm lining of the jaws that seals around the necks of the teeth.

lips.description: The lips surround the mouth. They are used in speech, eating and facial expression.

pituitary.description: A pea-sized gland under the brain that controls many other glands through the hormones it releases.

pineal.description: A small gland in the middle of the brain that releases melatonin, which helps set the daily sleep–wake rhythm.

pancreatic-duct.description: Carries digestive juice from the pancreas to the duodenum.

cortex.description: A fold of the cerebral cortex. The folds greatly increase its surface area; different gyri specialize in movement, sensation, language, vision and planning.

brain-lobe.description: A lobe of the cerebral hemisphere.

cerebellum.description: Coordinates movement, balance and posture, and fine-tunes motor learning.

brainstem.description: The brainstem connects the brain to the spinal cord and controls breathing, heart rate and many reflexes.

diencephalon.description: Deep structures around the third ventricle. The thalamus relays sensory information to the cortex; the hypothalamus controls hunger, thirst, temperature and hormones.

basal.description: Deep gray matter involved in starting and controlling movement and in habits and reward.

limbic.description: Part of the limbic system, involved in memory and emotion.

white-matter.description: Bundles of nerve fibers connecting different parts of the brain.

ventricle.description: A space inside the brain filled with cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions the brain and carries nutrients and waste.

choroid.description: Tufts of blood vessels in the ventricles that produce cerebrospinal fluid.

optic.description: Carries visual signals from the eye. The two optic nerves meet at the optic chiasm, where half of the fibers cross, and continue as the optic tracts.

colliculus.description: A small mound on the back of the midbrain. The superior colliculi help steer the eyes; the inferior colliculi relay hearing.

artery.description: An artery. Its thick muscular wall carries blood away from the heart under high pressure.

aorta.description: The largest artery. It leaves the left ventricle, arches over the heart and runs down through the chest and abdomen, giving branches to the whole body.

coronary.description: The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself with blood.

pulmonary-artery.description: The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, branching to each lobe and then to each bronchopulmonary segment.

vein.description: A vein. Its thin wall carries blood back to the heart under low pressure.

vena-cava.description: The superior and inferior venae cavae return blood from the whole body to the right atrium.

pulmonary-vein.description: The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium, gathering it from each bronchopulmonary segment.

cardiac-vein.description: Drain blood from the heart muscle, mostly into the coronary sinus.

larynx-cartilage.description: The largest cartilage of the larynx. Its front edge forms the Adam's apple.

nasal-cartilage.description: The cartilages that shape the lower part of the nose.

cerebral-artery.description: One of the arteries that supply the brain. They arise from the internal carotid and vertebral arteries, which meet beneath the brain in the circle of Willis.

carotid.description: The carotid arteries supply the head and neck. Each common carotid divides into an internal branch for the brain and eye and an external branch for the face and scalp.

vertebral-artery.description: Runs up through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae to supply the back of the brain. The two vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery.

jugular.description: The jugular veins drain the head and neck into the subclavian veins.

portal-vein.description: The portal system carries nutrient-rich blood from the stomach, intestines, pancreas and spleen to the liver before it returns to the heart.

hepatic-vein.description: The hepatic veins drain blood from the liver into the inferior vena cava.

limb-artery.description: An artery of the limb. Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure; in the limbs they run deep, alongside the bones and between the muscles.

limb-vein.description: A vein of the limb. The deep veins accompany the arteries; the superficial veins run just under the skin and are the ones seen through it.

cornea.description: The clear front window of the eye. It does most of the focusing; the lens behind it does the fine adjustment.

lens.description: A clear, flexible disc behind the pupil. The ciliary muscle changes its shape to focus on near or far objects; it stiffens with age, which is why reading glasses become necessary.

iris.description: The colored ring of muscle around the pupil, which it widens in dim light and narrows in bright light.

sclera.description: The tough white outer coat of the eyeball, to which the eye muscles attach.

eye-choroid.description: A layer rich in blood vessels between the sclera and the retina that feeds the outer retina.

ciliary.description: A ring of muscle and folds behind the iris. It focuses the lens through the suspensory ligament and makes the fluid that fills the front of the eye.

vitreous.description: The clear gel and fluid that fill the eyeball: the aqueous humor in front of the lens and the vitreous body behind it.

retina.description: The light-sensitive lining of the back of the eye, which turns light into nerve signals carried by the optic nerve.

eye-muscle.description: One of the small muscles that move the eye or lift the eyelid. Four recti and two obliques turn the eyeball; they are the fastest muscles in the body.

cranial-nerve.description: A branch of the cranial nerves in the orbit. The ophthalmic nerve and its branches carry feeling from the eye, forehead and nose; the oculomotor and trochlear nerves drive the eye muscles.

ganglion.description: A small cluster of nerve cells behind the eye. Its fibers, through the short ciliary nerves, narrow the pupil and focus the lens.

dura.description: The tough outer membrane around the brain. The tentorium cerebelli is a fold of it that forms a tent over the cerebellum and holds up the back of the cerebrum.

tongue.description: A muscular organ for tasting, chewing, swallowing and speaking. Its surface carries the papillae with the taste buds.

salivary.description: A salivary gland. With the parotid glands, the submandibular and sublingual glands make the saliva that moistens food and begins digesting starch.

tongue-muscle.description: An extrinsic muscle of the tongue. Genioglossus pushes the tongue forward and out; hyoglossus pulls it down.

pharynx-muscle.description: A muscle of the pharynx or soft palate. The constrictors squeeze swallowed food downward; the palate muscles seal off the nose and open the auditory tube when swallowing.

larynx-muscle.description: One of the small muscles of the larynx that move its cartilages to open, close and tense the vocal cords, for breathing, swallowing and speech.

laryngeal-cartilage.description: A cartilage of the larynx. The ring-shaped cricoid sits below the thyroid cartilage, and the small arytenoids on top of it pivot to open and close the vocal cords.

epiglottis.description: A leaf of elastic cartilage behind the tongue that tips back over the entrance of the larynx when swallowing, so food goes down the esophagus and not into the airway.

heart-cavity.description: The space inside a chamber of the heart, shown as the volume of blood it holds. Hidden by default so the valves stay visible; show it from the list.

layers.name: Skin and hair
layers.description: The skin is the largest organ of the body, a waterproof, self-repairing barrier that also senses touch and heat and helps control body temperature.

layers.name: Muscles and tendons
layers.description: Skeletal muscles pull on bones through tendons to move joints and hold posture, down to the muscles that move the eyes, the tongue, the soft palate and the vocal cords. Tendons, ligaments and fasciae are shown in a paler color.

layers.name: Organs
layers.description: The internal organs of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, the heart chamber by chamber and valve by valve, the bronchial tree, the eyes with their lens, iris and retina, the tear glands, the tongue and salivary glands, the ears, lips and gums.

layers.name: Arteries
layers.description: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. The aorta and its branches to the trunk, the limbs and the head, down to the arteries of the fingers, toes and brain, with the coronary arteries and the pulmonary arteries to each segment of the lungs.

layers.name: Veins
layers.description: Veins return blood to the heart. The venae cavae and the deep and superficial veins of the limbs, the veins of the heart and lungs, and the portal system that carries blood from the gut to the liver.

layers.name: Brain and nerves
layers.description: The brain with its gyri, deep nuclei and fluid-filled ventricles, the tentorium, the optic nerves and the nerves of the orbit. The spinal cord and the peripheral nerves of the body are not part of this dataset.

layers.name: Cartilage
layers.description: Intervertebral discs, costal cartilages, the cartilages of the larynx with the epiglottis, and the cartilages of the nose.

about.intro: A complete adult male body built from real anatomical surface models: skin, muscles, organs, the brain, the arteries and veins and every bone, down to the parts of the eye, the cartilages of the larynx and each cusp of the heart valves. Each structure is a separate object you can select, fade, hide, isolate and pull apart.
gaps: Nerves: the brain, the optic nerves and the nerves of the orbit are modeled, but not the spinal cord or the peripheral nerves of the body.
Vessels: the arteries and veins stop at the fingers and toes. In the head the arteries of the brain are modeled, but not its veins or the vessels of the face and scalp.
Organs: the liver, the colon and the small intestine are single structures without their segments.
Bones: the coccyx, the six ear ossicles and the third molars are missing from the dataset.
The lymphatic system and female anatomy are not part of this model. Bones are outer surfaces only, without marrow.
